title: Exchange Rates, Taxes and Development
bigQuestion: What decides how far a dollar goes, at home, at the border and around the world?

story.title: The Number on the Airport Board
story.kicker: A family lands in Mexico City with $800 and discovers that how much it buys depends on a number that changed while they were in the air.
paragraphs: The Reyes family from Aurora, Illinois, saved for a year to visit relatives in Mexico City. They took $800 in cash for the trip, on top of the plane tickets. When they walked past the exchange counter at the airport, the board showed a rate: 1 U.S. dollar equals 20 pesos. Their $800 would become 16,000 pesos. The kids did the math on their phones and felt rich.

Their aunt met them at the arrivals hall and told them not to exchange at the airport, where the counter takes a cut. At a bank in the city the rate was a little better. But she also said something that stuck with the older daughter, Elena. Last year, she said, the rate was 17 pesos to the dollar. Your $800 would have been only 13,600 pesos then. This year the dollar is strong, so your trip is cheap. Elena asked why the number had moved. Her aunt laughed and said nobody really knows.

Someone does know, at least in outline. A currency is bought and sold like anything else, and its price moves for reasons economics can trace: interest rates, what people expect, how much of each country's goods the other wants to buy. A strong dollar made the Reyes family's trip cheaper. It also made every Illinois soybean more expensive for a buyer in Mexico, and every avocado in a Chicago grocery a little cheaper.

On the last day, Elena's uncle asked what she paid in taxes back home. She had a part-time job at a grocery store and had noticed that her paycheck was smaller than her hours times her wage. She could name the lines on the pay stub but not what each one paid for. Her uncle, who ran a small shop, said he could tell her exactly what he paid and to whom. Neither of them could say who paid more as a share of what they earned.

This last chapter of the course puts those two conversations together and adds a third. How does a dollar's value abroad get set, and who wins when it moves? How do different kinds of taxes fall on different people? And the biggest question of all: why is a family in Aurora so much richer, on average, than most families in most of the world, and what would it take to change that?
story.think: The strong dollar made the family's trip cheaper. Who in Illinois might have been hurt by the very same change?

lessons.title: What an Exchange Rate Is
lessons.mainIdea: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, and when the dollar strengthens, foreign goods and trips get cheaper for Americans.
reading: An *exchange rate* is the price of one country's money measured in another country's money. If 1 dollar buys 20 pesos, the exchange rate is 20 pesos per dollar. You can flip it: 1 peso buys 1/20 of a dollar, or 5 cents. Every day, banks, businesses and travelers exchange trillions of dollars' worth of currencies, and the rates move minute by minute like stock prices.

Work through a meal. A restaurant in Mexico City charges 300 pesos for dinner. At 20 pesos per dollar, that dinner costs an American 300 divided by 20, or $15. Now suppose the rate moves to 15 pesos per dollar. The same 300-peso dinner costs 300 divided by 15, or $20. Nothing changed in the restaurant. The dollar simply buys fewer pesos, so everything priced in pesos costs more dollars.

When a dollar buys more foreign money than before, we say the dollar has *appreciated*, or gotten stronger. When it buys less, it has *depreciated*, or weakened. Students often get the direction backwards, so check with the meal. At 20 pesos per dollar the dinner was $15; at 15 pesos per dollar it was $20. More pesos per dollar means a stronger dollar and cheaper foreign goods for Americans.

The same logic runs the other way for a Mexican traveler in Chicago. A $40 museum ticket costs 800 pesos when the rate is 20, but only 600 pesos when the rate is 15. A weaker dollar is a stronger peso, and it makes American goods cheaper for Mexicans. Every exchange rate is two prices at once, and whatever one side gains in cheapness, the other side loses.

words.d: the price of one country's currency measured in another country's currency
to rise in value; a currency appreciates when it buys more of another currency than before
to fall in value; a currency depreciates when it buys less of another currency than before
the money used in a particular country, such as the dollar, the peso or the euro

look.title: One Dinner, Four Exchange Rates (Example)
look.cite: Labeled example: 300 pesos divided by the exchange rate
look.prompt: As the number of pesos per dollar falls, what happens to the dollar cost? In which row is the dollar strongest?

check.q: A hotel in Mexico costs 1,800 pesos a night. At 18 pesos per dollar, what is the dollar cost?
check.why: 1,800 pesos divided by 18 pesos per dollar is $100.

check.q: The rate moves from 18 pesos per dollar to 20 pesos per dollar. The dollar has
choices: depreciated, making trips to Mexico more expensive
appreciated, making trips to Mexico cheaper
appreciated, making trips to Mexico more expensive
check.why: A dollar now buys more pesos, so it appreciated, and peso prices cost fewer dollars.

check.q: If the dollar weakens against the euro, a European tourist in Chicago finds American prices
check.why: A weaker dollar is a stronger euro, so each euro buys more dollars and American goods cost fewer euros.

lessons.title: Exporters and Importers
lessons.mainIdea: A stronger dollar helps American importers and consumers of foreign goods but hurts American exporters, and a weaker dollar does the reverse.
reading: Think of an Illinois soybean farmer selling to a buyer in Mexico. Suppose soybeans sell for $10 a bushel. At 20 pesos per dollar the Mexican buyer pays 200 pesos a bushel. If the dollar strengthens to 25 pesos, the same $10 bushel costs the buyer 250 pesos. Nothing about the beans changed, but they got 25% more expensive in Mexico. The buyer may switch to Brazilian soybeans instead. A strong dollar makes American *exports* harder to sell.

Now think of a Chicago store that imports avocados priced at 40 pesos each. At 20 pesos per dollar, each avocado costs the store $2. At 25 pesos per dollar it costs $1.60. The store can lower its price and sell more. A strong dollar makes *imports* cheaper, which is good for stores that sell them, for factories that use imported parts, and for every shopper who buys foreign goods.

So the same event, a stronger dollar, creates winners and losers inside the country. Winners: importers, consumers, travelers going abroad and businesses that buy foreign inputs. Losers: exporters such as farmers and machinery makers, American hotels and attractions that serve foreign tourists, and firms that compete with imports at home. A weaker dollar flips every one of those. That is why you will hear a business leader complain about the strong dollar while a shopper next to her enjoys cheap electronics.

Because a strong dollar makes exports fall and imports rise, it tends to push the trade balance toward a larger deficit. A weak dollar tends to shrink the deficit. This connects the two halves of the unit. When you read that the dollar has risen, ask who sells abroad and who buys from abroad, and you will know who is smiling.

words.d: goods and services produced at home and sold to buyers in other countries
goods and services produced abroad and bought by people and businesses at home
a dollar that buys more foreign currency than before; it makes imports cheaper and exports dearer

look.title: One Factory, Two Currencies
look.text: A Rockford company builds machine tools and sells 40% of them to buyers in Europe. It also buys motors from a German supplier. Over a year the dollar strengthens sharply against the euro. The sales manager and the purchasing manager both walk into the same meeting, one frowning and one smiling.
look.prompt: Which manager is which, and why? What could the company do to reduce how much exchange rate swings matter to it?

check.q: A $50 Illinois product sells in Mexico. The rate moves from 20 to 25 pesos per dollar. Its peso price goes from
choices: 1,000 pesos to 1,250 pesos, so it is harder to sell
1,250 pesos to 1,000 pesos, so it is easier to sell
1,000 pesos to 1,250 pesos, so it is easier to sell
check.why: $50 times 20 is 1,000 pesos; $50 times 25 is 1,250 pesos. A higher peso price makes the export harder to sell.

check.q: Which group gains from a weaker dollar?
choices: Chicago factories that buy foreign parts
check.why: A weak dollar makes American goods cheaper in foreign currency, so exporters sell more.

check.q: A stronger dollar tends to push the U.S. trade balance
choices: toward a smaller deficit, since imports fall
toward a larger deficit, since imports get cheaper and exports get pricier
check.why: A strong dollar makes imports cheaper and exports more expensive abroad, so imports rise and exports fall.

lessons.title: Why Exchange Rates Move
lessons.mainIdea: A currency's price is set by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market, driven by trade, interest rates and expectations.
reading: A currency is bought and sold in a market, so its price obeys supply and demand. Who demands dollars? Anyone abroad who wants to buy American things: a Mexican company buying Illinois soybeans, a Japanese investor buying a Treasury bond, a tourist booking a hotel in Chicago. They must sell their own currency and buy dollars. When demand for dollars rises, the dollar appreciates, just as the price of anything rises when more people want it.

Who supplies dollars? Americans who want foreign things: a store importing avocados, an investor buying European stocks, the Reyes family exchanging $800 for pesos. They sell dollars and buy foreign currency. When Americans want more from abroad, the supply of dollars in the market grows, and the dollar depreciates. Trace any news story about the dollar back to one of these two curves.

Interest rates are the biggest short-run driver. If the Federal Reserve raises interest rates while other central banks do not, dollar bonds and bank accounts pay more. Investors around the world want them, so demand for dollars rises and the dollar appreciates. A rate cut does the reverse. Expectations matter too: if traders expect the dollar to rise next month, they buy it now, which makes it rise today. And a country with high inflation tends to see its currency depreciate over time, because each unit buys less.

Most major currencies, including the dollar, *float*: their prices move freely with the market. Some countries instead *peg* their currency, promising to hold it at a fixed rate to the dollar, and their central banks buy or sell reserves to keep it there. A peg gives businesses certainty but can break badly if the market pushes hard enough. The value of the dollar is also lifted by a special role: much of world trade and many foreign reserves are held in dollars, which creates steady demand for it.

words.d: the worldwide market where currencies are bought and sold
to let a currency's exchange rate be set freely by supply and demand
to fix a currency's exchange rate to another currency, with the central bank buying and selling to hold it there
the price of borrowing money, stated as a percent of the amount borrowed per year

look.title: Three Headlines
look.text: Headline one: the Federal Reserve raises its interest rate target while Europe holds steady. Headline two: a record harvest lets Illinois farmers export far more grain than usual. Headline three: American shoppers buy a record number of imported cars. Each headline changes either the demand for dollars or the supply of dollars in the foreign exchange market.
look.prompt: For each headline, say which curve moves, which way, and whether the dollar appreciates or depreciates as a result.

check.q: A Japanese investor buys U.S. Treasury bonds. In the foreign exchange market this
choices: has no effect on the dollar
check.why: To buy an American asset the investor must buy dollars, adding to demand for dollars.

check.q: If the Fed raises interest rates while other central banks hold steady, the dollar most likely
choices: appreciates, because investors want higher-paying dollar assets
check.why: Higher U.S. rates attract foreign investors, raising demand for dollars and pushing its price up.

check.q: What does it mean that the dollar floats?
choices: Its exchange rate is set by supply and demand in the market
Its value is fixed by law at a set number of pesos
It can only be used at sea
check.why: A floating currency's price moves freely with buying and selling; a pegged one is held fixed.

lessons.title: Progressive, Regressive, Proportional
lessons.mainIdea: A tax is progressive, regressive or proportional depending on whether the share of income it takes rises, falls or stays the same as income rises.
reading: Governments raise money in many ways, and economists sort taxes by one question: as a person's income rises, does the tax take a bigger share of it, a smaller share, or the same share? Notice the word share. A rich person almost always pays more dollars than a poor person. What matters for this sorting is the percent of income paid, which economists call the *average tax rate*: total tax divided by total income.

Take two people, one earning $20,000 a year and one earning $100,000. Under a *progressive tax*, the share rises with income. Suppose the first person pays $1,000 and the second pays $20,000. The first pays 5% of income; the second pays 20%. The federal income tax works this way, with higher rates applied to income above certain levels. Under a *proportional tax*, sometimes called a flat tax, everyone pays the same share. At a flat 5%, the first pays $1,000 and the second pays $5,000. Illinois's state income tax is proportional, a single rate of 4.95% on income.

Under a *regressive tax*, the share falls as income rises, even though dollars may rise. Sales taxes usually work this way. Suppose both people spend $10,000 a year on taxed goods and the sales tax is 6%. Each pays $600. For the first person that is 3% of income; for the second it is 0.6%. Lower-income households spend a bigger part of what they earn, so a tax on spending takes a bigger share from them.

Two cautions. First, a tax can look progressive on paper and be less so in practice, because deductions and exemptions change who pays. Second, judging a tax system means adding all the taxes together, since a regressive sales tax and a progressive income tax partly offset each other. Economists describe the shape of a tax with these words. Whether a tax should be more or less progressive is a question of values on which reasonable people, and economists, disagree.

words.d: total tax paid divided by total income, expressed as a percent
a tax that takes a larger share of income from higher-income people than from lower-income people
a tax that takes the same share of income from everyone; also called a flat tax
a tax that takes a smaller share of income from higher-income people than from lower-income people

look.title: Three Taxes on Two Incomes (Example)
look.prompt: Compute the average tax rate for each row. Which tax is progressive, which is regressive and which is proportional?

check.q: Ana earns $30,000 and pays $1,500 in a tax. Ben earns $90,000 and pays $9,000. This tax is
check.why: Ana pays 5% of income; Ben pays 10%. The share rises with income, which is progressive.

check.q: Why is a sales tax usually considered regressive?
choices: Because rich people pay no sales tax
Because lower-income households spend a larger share of income, so the tax takes a larger share from them
Because the rate falls as purchases grow
Because it is collected by states
check.why: Everyone pays the same rate per purchase, but spending is a bigger share of a low income.

check.q: A flat 4.95% state income tax on all income is an example of a
check.why: A single rate on all income takes the same share from everyone, which is proportional.

lessons.title: Income and Payroll Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: Income taxes fund general government and rise with income in steps; payroll taxes fund Social Security and Medicare and come straight out of each paycheck.
reading: Look at a pay stub and you will see several lines subtracted from gross pay. The largest for most workers is federal *income tax*. Congress created the modern version after the Sixteenth Amendment was ratified in 1913. The tax uses *brackets*: a low rate on the first slice of income, a higher rate on the next slice, and so on. A common mistake is to think that moving into a higher bracket taxes all your income at the higher rate. Only the dollars inside that bracket are taxed at that rate.

Here is the bracket idea with made-up rates. Suppose the first $10,000 of income is taxed at 10% and everything above that at 20%. A person earning $15,000 pays $1,000 on the first $10,000 plus $1,000 on the next $5,000, for $2,000 total. Her average tax rate is $2,000 divided by $15,000, about 13%. Her *marginal tax rate*, the rate on her next dollar, is 20%. A raise never leaves you with less take-home pay under a bracket system, because only the extra dollars face the higher rate.

The next lines are *payroll taxes*, listed as Social Security and Medicare, or together as FICA. The Social Security tax takes 6.2% of wages up to a yearly cap, and Medicare takes 1.45% with no cap. On a $1,000 paycheck that is $62 plus $14.50, or $76.50. Your employer pays a matching amount on top of your wages. These taxes fund retirement and disability benefits and health insurance for people over 65. Because the Social Security portion stops above the cap, payroll taxes as a whole are regressive at high incomes, though the benefits they fund are tilted toward lower earners.

Illinois adds its own flat income tax at 4.95%, so an Illinois pay stub has a state line too. Put together, a worker's paycheck shrinks by federal income tax, state income tax and payroll taxes before she sees it. The amounts withheld are estimates. In the spring, filing a tax return settles the account: a refund if too much was withheld, a payment if too little.

words.d: a tax on the money a person or business earns during the year
a range of income taxed at one rate; higher brackets apply higher rates only to the dollars inside them
the tax rate paid on the next dollar of income earned
a tax taken from wages to fund Social Security and Medicare, matched by the employer

look.title: The Amendment Behind the Income Tax
look.text: The Congress shall have power to lay and collect taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived, without apportionment among the several States, and without regard to any census or enumeration.
look.cite: Sixteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution, ratified 1913
look.prompt: Before this amendment, a federal income tax had been struck down by the Supreme Court. Why might a country need a new kind of tax as its government grew?

check.q: The first $10,000 of income is taxed at 10% and income above that at 20%. How much tax does a person earning $25,000 owe?
On a $2,000 paycheck, how much is withheld for Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) combined?
A worker gets a raise that moves her into a higher tax bracket. What happens?
choices: All her income is now taxed at the higher rate
Only the income inside the new bracket is taxed at the higher rate
check.why: Brackets apply marginal rates to slices of income, so a raise always increases take-home pay.

lessons.title: Sales and Property Taxes
lessons.mainIdea: Sales taxes fund states and cities through spending, and property taxes fund schools and local services through the value of land and buildings.
reading: Buy a $40 pair of shoes in Illinois and the register adds *sales tax*. The state's base rate is 6.25%, and counties, cities and transit districts often add more, so the total in Chicago is higher than in a small downstate town. At 6.25%, the tax on $40 shoes is $2.50 and the total is $42.50. Sales tax is easy to collect, since stores do it at the register, and it is the largest source of money for many states. As you saw, it is regressive, which is why some states exempt groceries or medicine.

Own a house and you pay *property tax* each year, based on the *assessed value* of the land and building. Suppose a home is assessed at $200,000 and the local rate is 2%. The owner pays $4,000 a year. Renters pay it indirectly, because landlords build it into rent. In Illinois, property taxes are among the higher ones in the country, and they are the main source of money for local public schools. This is why school funding differs so much between towns with expensive homes and towns with cheap ones.

Governments also charge *excise taxes* on particular goods: gasoline, tobacco, alcohol. A gasoline tax of, say, 40 cents a gallon adds $6 to a 15-gallon fill-up. Excise taxes often do two jobs: raising money and discouraging the thing taxed. A gasoline tax that pays for roads charges the people who use them most. A tobacco tax raises money and lowers smoking, which is the externality idea from earlier in the course.

Every tax has three questions attached. What does it fund? Who actually bears it, remembering that the person who writes the check may pass the cost along? And what behavior does it change? A property tax that funds schools, falls partly on renters and encourages nobody to do anything different is a very different instrument from a tobacco tax that funds health programs, falls on smokers and reduces smoking. Sorting taxes this way is the economic way of thinking applied to government.

words.d: a tax added to the price of goods at the time of purchase, collected by the seller for the government
a yearly tax on the assessed value of land and buildings, used mainly to fund local schools and services
the value a local government assigns to a property for the purpose of taxing it
a tax on a specific good, such as gasoline or tobacco, often per unit rather than as a percent of price

look.title: Two Towns, Two Schools
look.text: Town A has homes assessed at an average of $400,000; Town B's average $150,000. Both tax property at 2% to fund their schools, and both have 1,000 homes. Work out how much each town raises. Then consider what Town B could do: raise its rate, ask the state for help, or accept smaller budgets.
look.prompt: How much more does Town A raise? Why does funding schools with property tax lead to unequal schools, and what are the trade-offs of each fix?

check.q: A jacket costs $80 and the sales tax rate is 6.25%. What is the total at the register?
check.why: 6.25% of $80 is $5, so the total is $85.00.

check.q: A home is assessed at $250,000 and the property tax rate is 2%. The yearly tax is
Which tax is the main source of money for Illinois public schools?
check.why: Local property taxes fund most of the budget of Illinois school districts.

lessons.title: Measuring Development
lessons.mainIdea: Economists compare countries by GDP per capita adjusted for prices, plus health and schooling, and the gaps between rich and poor countries are enormous.
reading: The average American produces and earns far more than the average person in most of the world. The usual measure is *GDP per capita*: a country's total output divided by its population. The United States produces on the order of $80,000 per person per year. Some of the poorest countries produce less than $1,000 per person. Even after adjusting for the fact that food and housing cost less in poor countries, the gap is many times over. That gap, and what causes it, is the subject of *economic development*.

GDP per capita is an average and hides a lot, so economists add other measures. Life expectancy at birth tells you about health. Years of schooling and literacy tell you about education. Access to electricity, clean water and the internet tells you about daily life. The United Nations combines income, health and schooling into a single number called the *Human Development Index*, so that a country with a high income but poor health does not look better than it should.

Here is the hopeful part of the story. In 1990 roughly 4 in 10 people in the world lived in *extreme poverty*, which the World Bank defines as living on only a few dollars a day. By 2019 it was under 1 in 10. Most of that change came from fast growth in Asia, above all in China and India, where hundreds of millions of people moved from farms to factories and cities. The pandemic in 2020 pushed the number back up for a time, and progress in parts of Africa has been much slower.

A pattern to remember: small differences in growth rates become huge differences over decades. A country growing 2% a year doubles its income in about 35 years. A country growing 7% a year doubles in about 10 years. Over a working lifetime, the second country goes from poor to middle income while the first barely moves. So the question of development is really the question of what makes a country grow faster, year after year.

words.d: a country's gross domestic product divided by its population; output per person
the process by which a country raises its people's income, health and education over time
a United Nations measure that combines income, life expectancy and schooling into one score
living on only a few dollars a day, the World Bank's line for the world's poorest people

look.title: Share of the World in Extreme Poverty
look.cite: World Bank estimates, rounded to whole percents
look.prompt: By how many percentage points did the share fall from 1990 to 2019? What would you need to know to say how many people that was?

check.q: A country has a GDP of $600 billion and a population of 30 million. Its GDP per capita is
check.why: $600,000,000,000 divided by 30,000,000 people is $20,000 per person.

check.q: Why do economists add life expectancy and schooling to GDP per capita when comparing countries?
choices: Because GDP per capita cannot be calculated for poor countries
Because health and education are not part of the economy
Because an average income can hide poor health or education
check.why: GDP per capita is only an average of output. Health and schooling show how people actually live.

check.q: What happened to the share of the world living in extreme poverty between 1990 and 2019?
choices: It fell from roughly 4 in 10 to under 1 in 10
check.why: Fast growth, especially in Asia, cut the extreme poverty share from around 38% to under 10%.

lessons.title: Why Some Countries Grow
lessons.mainIdea: Countries grow when they build capital, educate and keep healthy their workers, adopt technology and trade, and the institutions that protect property and enforce contracts make all of that possible.
reading: Output per worker rises when each worker has more to work with. *Physical capital* means machines, roads, ports, power plants and factories. A farmer with a tractor grows far more than one with a hoe. Building capital requires saving and investing, either by a country's own people or by foreigners, which is one reason capital flows across borders matter. *Human capital* means the skills, knowledge and health of the workers themselves. A literate, healthy workforce can use better tools and learn new ones.

Technology multiplies both. The same worker with the same machine produces more when someone finds a better method, a better seed or a better way to organize the factory. Poor countries have an advantage here: they can adopt what rich countries already invented instead of discovering it themselves. That is how several Asian economies caught up so fast. Trade speeds the process, because it brings in machines and ideas and forces domestic firms to match the world's best.

But many countries have savings, workers and access to technology and still stay poor. The missing piece is *institutions*: the rules of the game. Will the government or a powerful neighbor seize your farm if you improve it? Will a court enforce a contract with a stranger? Can a business get a license without paying a bribe? Where property is secure, contracts hold and corruption is limited, people invest and build. Where they are not, people hide wealth, keep businesses small and stay away from long-term plans.

Economists disagree about how much weight to give each ingredient and about the best policies to build them. Some emphasize open trade and markets, some emphasize public investment in schools and roads, some emphasize political stability first. Almost all agree on a few things. War and civil conflict destroy growth. Hyperinflation destroys it. Educating girls as well as boys pays off in every measure. And there is no case of a country becoming rich while cut off from the rest of the world.

words.d: the machines, buildings, roads and equipment used to produce goods and services
the skills, education, experience and health that make workers productive
the laws, courts, customs and government rules that shape how people can own, trade and invest
the legal protection of a person's right to own, use and sell what belongs to them

look.title: Two Farmers, Same Soil
look.text: Two farmers on opposite sides of a border work identical land. One holds a legal title to her field, can borrow against it and knows a court will back her if a buyer refuses to pay. The other has farmed his field for thirty years but has no title; officials could reassign it, and a lender will not accept it as collateral. Each is offered the chance to spend a year's savings on an irrigation system that pays off over ten years.
look.prompt: Which farmer invests, and why? What does this suggest about why some countries with good land and hard-working people stay poor?

check.q: Which of these is an example of human capital?
check.why: Human capital is the skill and knowledge in workers themselves; the others are physical capital.

check.q: Why can a poor country sometimes grow faster than a rich one?
choices: Because it has more money to invest
Because it invents more new technology
Because it can adopt technology that already exists instead of inventing it
check.why: Catching up is faster than pioneering. Adopting proven methods and machines lets output jump quickly.

check.q: A country has savings, educated workers and access to technology but people rarely start businesses or invest long term. The most likely missing ingredient is
choices: secure property rights and reliable courts
check.why: Without institutions that protect property and enforce contracts, investing is too risky, so people hold back.

lessons.title: Poverty and Inequality
lessons.mainIdea: Poverty is measured against a line of minimum income and inequality by how income is spread across groups, and they are different problems with different remedies.
reading: Poverty and inequality are related but not the same. *Poverty* is about having too little. The United States sets a *poverty line*, an income below which a household is counted as poor, adjusted for family size. For a family of four it has been around $30,000 a year in recent years. In recent years roughly 11 to 12 percent of Americans have lived below the line, with higher rates for children and for some groups. Government programs such as food assistance, tax credits for working families and housing aid are not counted in the official measure, so a second measure that includes them shows lower poverty.

*Inequality* is about how far apart incomes are, whether or not anyone is poor. A simple way to see it is to line up every household by income and cut the line into five equal groups, called *quintiles*. In an example economy, the bottom fifth might receive 4% of all income while the top fifth receives 50%. Economists also use a single number, the Gini index, that runs from 0, where everyone has the same income, to 100, where one person has everything. The United States has higher inequality than most other rich countries and lower than many developing ones.

The two can move in different directions. Fast growth can lift millions out of poverty while the richest gain even faster, so poverty falls and inequality rises. That is roughly what happened in China. A deep recession can leave inequality unchanged while poverty rises, because everyone loses together. When you read a claim about the economy, ask which of the two it is about.

What to do is one of the most argued questions in economics and politics. Some emphasize growth, since a growing economy has lifted more people out of poverty than any program. Some emphasize direct help, since growth can leave people behind for a long time. Economists broadly agree on a few points: education raises earnings, a strong job market is the best anti-poverty program, and how aid is designed matters, because a program that cuts off sharply when income rises can discourage work. How much to redistribute, and from whom, is a question of values that economics informs but cannot settle.

words.d: the condition of having too little income to afford a basic standard of living
the level of income below which a household is officially counted as poor, adjusted for family size
how unevenly income or wealth is spread across the people in a country
one fifth of the population when households are ranked from lowest to highest income

look.title: Share of Income by Fifth (Example Economy)
look.cite: Labeled example for this lesson; shares add to 100
look.prompt: How many times more income does the top fifth receive than the bottom fifth? If every household's income doubled, how would the shares change?

check.q: A country's poverty rate falls while its richest households pull far ahead of everyone else. Which is true?
check.why: Fewer people below the line means less poverty; a bigger gap at the top means more inequality.

check.q: In the example economy, the top fifth receives 50% of income and the bottom fifth 4%. The top fifth receives
check.why: 50 divided by 4 is 12.5.

check.q: Which statement about the U.S. poverty line is correct?
choices: It is the same for every household regardless of size
It is adjusted for family size, and about 11 to 12 percent of Americans have recently lived below it
check.why: The official line varies with family size and roughly one in nine Americans has fallen below it in recent years.

lessons.title: The Course in One Page
lessons.mainIdea: Every topic in this course comes back to a few habits: scarcity forces choices, choices have opportunity costs, people respond to incentives, and markets coordinate through prices.
reading: Everything you studied this year rests on one fact: *scarcity*. Wants are unlimited and resources are not, so every person, business and government must choose. Every choice has an *opportunity cost*, the next-best thing given up, and the honest way to think about any decision is to name that cost. A Saturday shift costs the game. A tariff on steel costs the machinery jobs. A dollar of tax spent on one program is a dollar not spent on another.

People respond to *incentives*, and most of what economics predicts follows from that. Raise the price of something and people buy less of it and make more of it; that is the law of demand and the law of supply. Put a ceiling under the price and you get a shortage; a floor over it and you get a surplus. Tax something and you get less of it, subsidize it and you get more. Whenever a policy surprises its designers, the usual reason is an incentive they did not see.

Markets coordinate millions of these choices through prices. A price is a signal that carries information nobody could gather on purpose: how much people want a thing and how hard it is to make. Where markets work, they push resources toward the uses people value most, and trade between people and between countries makes both sides better off. Where they fail, because of pollution, public goods, monopoly or missing information, government has a role, and that role has costs and limits of its own.

Finally, think at the *margin* and count everything. The question is rarely all or nothing; it is one more hour, one more unit, one more dollar, and whether its extra benefit beats its extra cost. Count the costs that are not on the price tag and the benefits that are not on the receipt. Keep sunk costs out of it. Measure the economy with GDP, the CPI and the unemployment rate, knowing what each one misses. These habits will not tell you what to value. They will tell you what your values cost.

words.d: the basic condition that wants are unlimited while the resources to satisfy them are limited
the next-best alternative given up when a choice is made
a reward or penalty that changes how people choose to act
the point of one more unit; thinking at the margin compares the extra benefit and extra cost of one more

look.title: Ten Ideas on One Card
look.text: Imagine you could hand a friend who never took this course a single index card. On it: scarcity, opportunity cost, incentives, supply and demand, equilibrium, market failure, GDP, inflation, unemployment, comparative advantage. Your friend asks you to explain the card using only one situation, such as a school deciding whether to add a second lunch period.
look.prompt: Pick your one situation and connect at least six of the ten ideas to it, with a number attached to each.

check.q: A city subsidizes rooftop solar panels and is surprised when installations triple. Which principle explains the result?
check.why: Lowering the cost of something leads people to do more of it; the subsidy changed the incentive.

check.q: Which best describes what a market price does?
choices: It signals how much people want a good and how costly it is to make
It is set by the government for every good
It measures the total output of the economy
check.why: A price carries information about demand and supply that no single planner could gather.

check.q: Thinking at the margin means asking
choices: whether to do all of something or none
whether one more unit's extra benefit beats its extra cost
what the average cost has been
check.why: Marginal thinking compares the benefit and cost of the next unit, not the whole or the past.

lessons.title: Applying the Model
lessons.mainIdea: Analyzing a real decision means naming the opportunity cost, tracing incentives, checking which way prices move and stating the trade-off before choosing.
reading: Take a decision that faces many high school seniors: go to a four-year college, go to community college, or work full time. Start with numbers. Suppose a full-time job pays $32,000 a year. A public university costs $15,000 a year in tuition and fees after aid, for four years. The tuition is only part of the cost. The opportunity cost of four years in college includes the $32,000 a year not earned, which adds up to $128,000. Total cost of the college path, tuition plus forgone earnings, is roughly $188,000.

Now the benefit. Suppose college graduates in the field you want earn $55,000 to start instead of $32,000, a difference of $23,000 a year. At that gap, the $188,000 cost is recovered in about 8 years of work, and the gains keep coming for decades after. The numbers are examples, and they change with the field, the school and the person. But the structure is always the same: cost, including opportunity cost, against benefit over time.

Then trace the incentives and the trade-offs. Community college for two years cuts tuition sharply and lets a student keep a part-time job, lowering the opportunity cost. Working first and studying later trades money now for a smaller lifetime gain. Borrowing to pay tuition adds interest, and a loan must be repaid whether or not the degree is finished. A student who is unsure of finishing faces a very different calculation from one who is certain. There is no single right answer, only a right way to think.

The same method works on any policy question in this course. A proposed tariff: name who pays, who gains, what happens to prices and to retaliation, and put a number on the cost per job. A minimum wage increase: trace what employers do, what workers gain, and what economists on each side predict. A tax change: ask who bears it and what behavior it changes. When you can do that, and then say which trade-off you would accept and why, you are thinking like an economist.

words.d: comparing all the costs of a choice, including opportunity cost, with all of its benefits over time
the income a person gives up by spending time in school or another activity instead of working
giving up some of one thing to get more of another

look.title: A Town Decides on a Factory
look.text: A company offers to build a plant in a small Illinois town with 300 jobs paying $50,000 a year, if the town gives it a property tax break worth $3 million a year for ten years. The plant will use river water and the town's roads. Some residents want the jobs; others point to the schools that property taxes fund and to the trucks on Main Street.
look.prompt: Name the opportunity cost of the tax break, the incentives on each side, and one number you would want before voting. Then argue for a decision.

check.q: A job pays $32,000 a year. Four years of college cost $15,000 a year in tuition. Counting forgone earnings, what is the total cost of the four years?
check.why: Tuition is 4 times $15,000, or $60,000; forgone earnings are 4 times $32,000, or $128,000. Together, $188,000.

check.q: Why does community college lower the opportunity cost of a degree?
choices: Because its graduates always earn more
Because it lets students keep working part time while paying less tuition
Because it has no cost at all
check.why: Lower tuition and the chance to keep earning reduce both the money paid and the earnings given up.

check.q: Which is the economic way to evaluate a proposed policy?
choices: Identify who pays, who gains, and what changes, then state the trade-off
Support it if a majority likes it
check.why: Economic analysis names costs and benefits for each group and the trade-off, then lets values decide.

review.q: A meal costs 500 pesos. At 20 pesos per dollar it costs $25. If the rate moves to 25 pesos per dollar, it costs
choices: $25, since the meal price did not change
review.why: 500 divided by 25 is $20. More pesos per dollar means a stronger dollar and cheaper foreign goods.

review.q: Which group is hurt by a stronger dollar?
review.why: A strong dollar makes American exports cost more in foreign currency, so exporters sell less.

review.q: If foreign investors rush to buy U.S. bonds after the Fed raises rates, the dollar will most likely
review.why: Buying U.S. bonds requires buying dollars, so demand for dollars rises and the dollar's price goes up.

review.q: Cara earns $40,000 and pays $4,000 in a tax; Dev earns $80,000 and pays $6,000. This tax is
review.why: Cara pays 10% of income and Dev pays 7.5%. The share falls as income rises, which is regressive.

review.q: Income up to $10,000 is taxed at 10% and above that at 20%. A person earning $40,000 pays
review.why: $1,000 on the first $10,000 plus 20% of $30,000, which is $6,000, totals $7,000.

review.q: Which tax is the largest source of funding for Illinois local public schools?
review.why: Local property taxes on assessed home and business values fund most of a school district's budget.

review.q: A country has good land, savings and educated workers, but officials can seize property and courts rarely enforce contracts. Economists would expect
choices: rapid growth, since the ingredients are all present
slow growth, because weak institutions discourage investment
review.why: Without secure property rights and reliable courts, people avoid long-term investment, so growth stalls.

review.q: If every household's income doubles, what happens to inequality measured by income shares?
choices: It stays the same, since every share is unchanged
review.why: Doubling every income leaves each fifth's share of the total exactly the same.
